notes: The “everlasting covenant” is not identified here. The accusation reaches beyond one city or social rank.
“West” and “east” render difficult expressions involving the sea and lights or fires. The call to honor the LORD extends across the world.
“Visited” can introduce punishment or attention leading to release. The verse does not explicitly settle the prisoners’ final outcome.
vocabulary: Covenant
A binding relationship with obligations; its violation is part of the chapter’s accusation.

notes: The same Hebrew verb describes swallowing up the covering and swallowing up death. “All peoples” and “all faces” give the promise its breadth.

The recorded reading has straw trampled “in” a dung pit; the written form mentions its waters. Moab’s spreading hands are compared to swimming, but the final expression about their skill is uncertain.
vocabulary: Aged wine
Wine left to mature on its sediment and then strained; part of the rich feast imagery.

notes: Verse 18’s “were born” can also be read “fell.” Verse 19 shifts from “your dead” to “my dead body,” with a plural verb; the corporate image is grammatically unusual. Its “dew of lights” is also rendered “dew of herbs.”
The statement that the dead will not rise in verse 14 and the promise that “your dead” will live in verse 19 address different groups. Their contrast is retained.
vocabulary: YAH
A shortened form of the divine name. The Hebrew places it alongside the full name rendered LORD.

notes: The pinned Hebrew describes a vineyard of delight. “A vineyard of wine,” found in some translations, reflects a different reading.
The language of measured expulsion is difficult, and the Hebrew shifts between “you,” “he,” and “her.” The draft retains those shifts rather than specifying every referent.
vocabulary: Leviathan
A named serpent-like sea creature in poetic imagery of divine victory.

notes: The repeated Hebrew sounds, tsav la-tsav and qav la-qav, can sound like elementary lessons or mocking babble. The quotation boundaries and speakers are interpretive choices.
The pinned Hebrew says the believer will not hurry or rush; “in panic” makes the sense explicit. It does not use the wording “be put to shame.”
vocabulary: Sheol
The realm of the dead. The “covenant with death” is the speakers’ image of supposed security.

notes: Ariel names the city where David camped. Its meaning is debated; the altar-hearth sense gives particular force to the threatened burning in verse 2.
The sealed document cannot be read by someone who knows how to read; the second recipient cannot read at all. The two obstacles are distinct.
vocabulary: Potter
A maker of clay vessels; the image asks whether the made thing can deny its maker’s understanding.

sections.1: Ariel and the Hidden Work of God

notes: “Rahab who sits still” mocks Egypt’s promised help. Rahab here belongs to the imagery of a powerful, boastful creature, not the woman in Joshua.
“Teacher” has a plural form but is paired with singular description; “teachers” is possible. The expression rendered “his burden heavy” in verse 27 may describe a heavy rising cloud or smoke.
vocabulary: Menstrual cloth
A cloth associated with menstrual impurity; the comparison expresses rejection of the plated images.

notes: The lion and hovering birds picture divine action around Zion. The wording about fighting “on” Mount Zion leaves the direction of that action less explicit than some translations do.
vocabulary: Flesh and spirit
The contrast here distinguishes mortal strength from divine power; it is not a claim that bodies are evil.

sections.1: Woe to Those Who Go Down to Egypt

notes: The address is to complacent women. The breast-beating and exposed bodies belong to the coming lament; they have not been changed into references to fields.
“Forever” in the description of desolation is followed by “until” the spirit is poured out. The poem’s reversal remains visible.
vocabulary: Spirit
Hebrew ruach can mean spirit, wind or breath. Here its pouring out from above brings renewal.

sections.1: A Righteous King and the Spirit from Above

notes: The prayer shifts from “their arm” to “our salvation,” and verse 6 shifts from “your times” to “his treasure.” The Hebrew’s changes of person are retained.
The pinned text says “cities.” A reading “witnesses” would make the line more explicitly legal, but is not substituted here.
vocabulary: Lawgiver
One who establishes binding rules; the title stands alongside judge and king.

sections.1: The LORD Is Exalted in Zion

notes: Several animal names are uncertain. Lilith is retained as the name of a night being; translating it as an ordinary owl would settle a disputed identification.
The Hebrew changes from “my mouth” to “his spirit.” The draft retains that shift rather than making both pronouns third person.
vocabulary: Emptiness and waste
The measuring imagery uses terms also found in the creation account’s description of the unformed earth.

notes: The final clause can mean that even fools will not lose their way, or that fools will not travel on this road. The draft takes it as an assurance about the way.
vocabulary: Ransomed
Released at a cost. The return song recurs almost word for word in Isaiah 51:11.

notes: The pinned text has “I say” in verse 5. In verse 10 it is the Assyrian spokesman who claims that the LORD commissioned the invasion.
The written Hebrew uses blunt words for excrement and urine; recorded reading traditions soften them. The threat of siege starvation remains explicit.
vocabulary: Rabshakeh
An Assyrian official’s title, retained rather than treated as a personal name.

notes: Verse 21 leaves its opening “because” clause suspended into the following message. Verse 27’s final field image is difficult; the pinned wording differs from the parallel in 2 Kings.
The stated total is 185,000. The account attributes the deaths to the LORD’s messenger without describing a medical cause.
vocabulary: Cherubim
Heavenly beings associated with the divine throne and sanctuary imagery.

sections.1: Hezekiah Prays and Jerusalem Is Delivered

notes: The Hebrew speaks of steps and a shadow, then of the sun going back ten steps. It does not specify the construction of a sundial.

Several lines of Hezekiah’s poem are compressed or difficult. “Waited” in verse 13 and “these things” in verse 16 remain uncertain. Verse 17 follows the wording of loving attachment rather than replacing it with “held back.”
vocabulary: Surety
Someone who guarantees another person’s case or obligation; the prayer asks the Lord to act in that role.

notes: Saris can describe a eunuch or a court official. The prospect is service in the Babylonian king’s palace; the bodily implication is not excluded.
vocabulary: Merodach-baladan
The Babylonian king who sends the delegation in this account.

notes: Verse 3 locates the road preparation in the wilderness. Verse 9 can address Zion as the herald or a herald bringing news to Zion; the draft takes Zion as the herald.
The pinned verb in verse 6 is “he says,” not “I said.” Its word for human faithfulness may also suggest constancy or beauty. Verse 20’s description of the idol-maker’s resources is uncertain.
vocabulary: Spirit
The Hebrew word can mean spirit, breath or wind. “Mind,” familiar from a Greek rendering, is not the pinned Hebrew wording.

sections.12: To Whom Will You Liken God?

notes: The victorious figure is not named in these verses. The north and the east are both retained; Cyrus is named later in 44:28.
The seven tree names are retained as a list. Several ancient plant identifications, especially the oil tree and the final three species, remain uncertain.
vocabulary: Redeemer
One who acts to recover or release another; the title draws on the language of family obligation.

sections.1: Do Not Fear, for I Am with You

notes: The servant is not given a personal name here. Verse 19 also calls a blind figure the servant; the relationship between these descriptions should not be resolved by inserting an identity into the text.
God is compared both to a male warrior and to a woman in labor. Verse 24 changes from “we” to “they”; that change remains.
vocabulary: Covenant
The servant is given “as a covenant,” not merely as someone who announces one.

sections.1: The Servant and a New Song

notes: The ransom language includes Egypt, Cush, Seba and other human lives. Its harsh implications are retained alongside the declaration of love for Israel.
Verse 14’s description of the fugitives and ships is uncertain. The “first father” in verse 27 is not named; the translation does not decide among proposed ancestors.
vocabulary: Blot out
Erase a record; the image connects forgiveness with no longer remembering the offenses.

notes: Writing “LORD’s” on the hand can also be understood as signing oneself over to the LORD. In verse 24 the recorded reading is “by myself”; the written form asks, “Who was with me?”
vocabulary: Jeshurun
A poetic name for Israel associated with being upright.

notes: “Anointed” explicitly describes Cyrus. The word rendered “disaster” can also mean evil; the verse attributes both well-being and calamity to the LORD.
Verse 11 can be punctuated as commands or as a challenge to those issuing commands to God. Verse 14 explicitly describes people arriving in chains.
vocabulary: Anointed
Marked out for a task or office, using the language of consecration with oil.

sections.1: Cyrus and the LORD Who Creates

notes: The images must be carried, while the LORD carries his people. The repeated verb creates the central contrast.
vocabulary: Bel and Nebo
Names of Babylonian deities whose images are pictured as burdens on animals.

sections.1: The Gods of Babylon and the God Who Carries

notes: “Spare no one” in verse 3 renders a difficult expression involving meeting or encountering a person. The expression rendered “charm it away” in verse 11 can also be connected with dawn or foreseeing disaster.
vocabulary: Daughter Babylon
The city and its people pictured as a woman; the forced labor and exposure describe her humiliation.

notes: “Judah’s waters” is the pinned image of descent. Verse 10 says “chosen”; “tested” would require a different Hebrew reading.
The final speaker is not identified. “And his Spirit” can mean that the Spirit also sends the speaker or that the Spirit is also sent.
vocabulary: Peace
Shalom includes security and well-being. The refrain returns in 57:21 with “my God” as the speaker’s designation.

notes: The servant is called Israel yet is commissioned to restore Israel. The draft preserves this tension. In verse 5 the recorded reading gathers Israel “to him”; the written form has “not.”
Verse 17 follows “children,” not the alternative “builders.” Verse 24’s pinned word means righteous or in the right; “tyrant” follows a different reading or interpretation.
vocabulary: Sinim
A distant land whose identification is uncertain.

sections.1: The Servant and the Restoration of Zion

notes: The learner’s tongue depends on a listening ear. The rare verb rendered “sustain” is uncertain, but the weary person and the spoken word are explicit.
vocabulary: Flint
A hard stone; setting the face like flint pictures determination despite abuse.

notes: “Die in the same way” can also be understood as “die like gnats.” Verse 19 names two paired calamities, then asks in the first person how to comfort the city.
vocabulary: Rahab
A sea-monster name in this poem’s image of divine victory, linked in the next verse with the sea crossing.
Hosts
Armies; the title “LORD of hosts” presents God as commander.

sections.1: Listen to Me, You Who Pursue Righteousness

notes: The servant’s wise action can also mean success. The poem shifts from “you” to “his.” “Sprinkle” follows the usual sense of the pinned verb; “startle” is a debated alternative.
vocabulary: Vessels
Objects used in sanctuary worship; their carriers are called to purity.

notes: “His generation” and the removal through oppression and judgment are disputed expressions. The suffix rendered “on him” can be plural, “on them.” Verse 9 has an unusual plural form, literally “in his deaths.”

The offering clause can mean “if you make his life” or “if his life makes.” “By his knowledge” may mean the servant’s knowledge or knowledge of him. The pinned text does not include “light” after “see,” though another textual reading does.
vocabulary: Reparation offering
Asham names guilt or an offering associated with addressing an offense. Its use here does not by itself settle every aspect of the servant’s identity or suffering.

notes: The pinned text has “Noah’s waters.” The city’s colored mortar, precious stones and architectural details are poetic; several material identifications are uncertain.
vocabulary: Covenant of peace
A binding promise of enduring well-being, set against mountains and hills that can move.

notes: The covenant is linked to the reliable acts of love promised to David. The passage moves from David as “him” to an unnamed singular “you.”
vocabulary: Word
Here God’s spoken purpose is pictured as a messenger that returns only after accomplishing its task.

notes: Foreigners and eunuchs are explicitly welcomed as covenant-keepers. The promise of a name “not cut off” answers the eunuch’s image of a dry tree.
vocabulary: Memorial and a name
Literally “a hand and a name”; a lasting place of remembrance, contrasted with remembrance through descendants.

sections.1: A House of Prayer for All Peoples

notes: “Nakedness” renders a sexual use of “hand,” though the expression is disputed. “King” follows the pinned vocalization; some understand the deity Molek.
Being taken away “from evil” can also mean “because of evil.” The “fruit of lips” pictures a response of speech or praise; the exact words are not supplied.
vocabulary: Crushed in spirit
People brought low inwardly; the high and holy one is said to dwell with them.

notes: The fast is criticized alongside exploitation of workers. Verse 10 says to give oneself, not simply food. “Talking business” in verse 13 interprets a broad expression, literally “speaking a word.”
vocabulary: Yoke
A wooden harness for working animals, used here for oppressive restraints imposed on people.

notes: The rare word rendered “vigorous” in verse 10 is uncertain. Verse 19 can also be read as an enemy coming like a flood and the LORD’s Spirit acting against him; the draft follows the rushing-river image of divine arrival.
vocabulary: Breastplate
Armor protecting the torso; righteousness, salvation, vengeance and zeal become the divine warrior’s clothing.

notes: The vision includes kings led in, destruction of nations that refuse service, and nursing at kings’ breasts. Those forceful and unusual images are retained.
vocabulary: Salvation and Praise
Names given to the restored city’s walls and gates.

notes: The prisoner-release expression can also suggest an opening of eyes. Verse 8 follows the pinned vocalization “in a burnt offering”; “with wrongdoing” is an alternative reading.
vocabulary: Headdress and ashes
The Hebrew words pe’er and ’efer sound alike; the exchange turns a sign of mourning into festive dress.

notes: The new names are translated for their meaning: Hephzibah, “My Delight Is in Her,” and Beulah, “Married.” Verse 5 retains the pinned “sons”; “builders” requires different vocalization.
vocabulary: Remind the LORD
The watchmen are charged with unceasing appeal, even giving God no rest until Jerusalem is established.

notes: Verse 9 follows the recorded reading “he was distressed”; the written “not” permits a different sense. The remembering subject in verse 11 is uncertain. Verse 17 directly asks why God causes wandering and hardening.
vocabulary: Winepress
A place where grapes are trodden; the poem transforms grape juice into the peoples’ lifeblood.

sections.1: The Day of Vengeance and the LORD's Steadfast Love

notes: Public 64:1 is the latter part of Hebrew 63:19; subsequent public labels in this chapter are one higher than Hebrew labels. Verse 5’s “in them” is difficult and may refer back to ways or sins; its question about salvation is not resolved here.
vocabulary: Menstrual cloth
An image of ritual impurity, retained in the community’s confession rather than generalized to dirt.

sections.1: A Prayer for the LORD to Come Down

notes: Verse 15 can quote a death curse or directly predict death. Verse 20 can describe someone failing to reach a hundred or a sinner a hundred years old. The vision still speaks of death; it has not been harmonized with other passages.
vocabulary: Fortune, Destiny, Amen
Fortune and Destiny name recipients of ritual meals. “God of Amen” identifies God with reliability and truth.

sections.1: New Heavens and a New Earth

notes: The paired acts in verse 3 can equate corrupt worship with violence or describe combined practices. The read form of “one” in verse 17 is feminine. Verse 18 opens with an incomplete clause; verse 21 does not explicitly identify everyone included in “them.”
vocabulary: All flesh
Humanity viewed as living, mortal beings; the book ends with both universal worship and a disturbing sight of judgment.

sections.1: The LORD Comes in Judgment and Glory
